The study evaluates the commercial qER EU 2.0 AI triage tool on non-contrast CT head scans without any training or fine-tuning, so no learning paradigm applies and the model is tagged verbatim per the evidence rules. Domain is clinical imaging evaluation of a diagnostic AI assistant.

The paper develops a machine-learning-accelerated molecular dynamics framework for the Cu-Ag catalyst, implying a supervised fit of an ML interatomic potential to reference data (e.g., DFT) used to drive MD simulations of surface segregation. The subject is computational/simulation chemistry of catalytic surfaces, with molecular dynamics and modelling as the tier-3 focus.

The paper trains multivariable logistic regression models on retrospective hospitalization data to predict 15-day and 30-day readmissions, a supervised prediction task in health services research. The subject is healthcare quality monitoring and risk management under payment reform, best captured by public health/epidemiology and medical informatics.

The paper trains physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) with physical constraints (Ekman momentum balance, shear/power-law constraint) embedded in the loss, supervised on LiDAR wind-profile data. Domains reflect atmospheric physics and machine learning applied to environmental wind monitoring; statistical tests like Kruskal-Wallis are excluded from model_type.

The paper trains a two-stage supervised cascade — a logistic regression sentinel and a random forest confirmer — on synchronized CT and welding-process data, so the domains are best captured under computer science/machine learning with no biomedical tier3 term applicable; the k-of-n temporal smoothing is a rule-based filter, not a learned model.

The paper trains a Gaussian Process Regression with Automatic Relevance Determination on Landsat-derived shoreline data with ERA5 climate predictors, a supervised non-neural statistical model. The subject is coastal/environmental forecasting with no biomedical domain match beyond the environmental science tier-2 term; ARD and permutation importance are feature-importance analyses, not model types.

Four supervised algorithms (SVM, linear regression, random forest, decision tree) were trained on soil-sample data to predict absorbed gamma dose rate, with random forest performing best; this is a supervised classical ML (ensemble) study in an environmental radiation (physics) domain. No deep learning, dimensionality reduction, or further tier-3 domain terms apply.

The paper trains random forest, gradient boosted regression trees and XGBoost models on halide perovskite descriptors to predict band gap energies, a supervised classical/ensemble ML study in computational materials chemistry. Feature importance analysis is an explainability step, not a separate model, and no deep learning or pretrained models are involved.

The study applies the existing LiSep LSTM (MIMIC-III-trained) to an external European cohort and additionally performs pooled training on combined data, a supervised septic-shock prediction task. Domains center on critical care medicine and medical informatics; permutation feature importance is an explainability method and is not tagged.

The paper trains a model zoo of logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting (LightGBM-style) on ECG-QRS event samples from PPG/ACC signals, with cross-subject nearest-neighbor geometry used for recoverability estimation. Domains reflect wearable cardiovascular signal analysis with a machine-learning methodology focus.

The paper develops a Basis-Driven Learnable Operator integrated into MLP-mixer vision architectures (CycleMLP, HireMLP, AS-MLP), all trained from scratch under supervised image classification on CIFAR and ImageNet datasets. The subject is computer science/machine learning rather than a biomedical domain, and Optuna and the Wilcoxon test are tuning/statistics, not model types.

domain_tier3: ["Protein folding, stability and design", "Structure prediction", "Small molecules"]

Chemistry paper using metadynamics molecular simulations of ZIF MOF polymorph selection plus neural network classifiers trained on databases of simulated synthesis structures; the metadynamics/force-field simulation is a physics method, so the only ML model is the supervised neural network classifier (no deep architecture stated).

The paper trains a Random Forest classifier on UHPLC-HRMS metabolite profiles to identify processing-dependent phenolic markers (SHAP is explainability, excluded), and uses hierarchical clustering as an unsupervised step to reveal chemotype structure. The subject is plant metabolomics applied to Asteraceae species and their secondary metabolites.

The paper trains an ensemble machine-learning prognostic model (supervised, but the abstract names no specific algorithm, so model_type keeps the paper's wording) and applies cell2location as-is for spatial mapping; CellChat, Monocle, pySCENIC, inferCNV, PROGENy and stLearn are analysis pipelines excluded from model typing. The subject is single-cell/spatial transcriptomics of colorectal cancer with CNV analysis.

The paper trains a knowledge-graph-based model using RGCN and GAT (both graph neural networks) on labelled gene-pair data to predict synthetic lethality, which is a supervised deep learning task applied to cancer genomics.

domain_tier3: ["Data submission, annotation and curation", "Data architecture, analysis and design"]

The only trained model is a LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression used to select and fit a five-gene diagnostic signature, i.e. supervised classical machine learning; WGCNA and immune-infiltration analyses are pipeline/statistical analyses, not models. The paper trains a 2D U-Net configured via nnU-Net v2 on expert-annotated laparoscopic video frames for supervised multiclass/binary semantic segmentation of the inferior mesenteric artery and vein. The subject is a surgical computer-vision support tool, so Medicine/Surgery/Medical informatics with Medical imaging capture the domain.

The paper develops a task-specific active-learning framework trained on sparse experimental data to discover low thermal expansion alloys; no specific algorithm is named beyond the active-learning setup, and 'machine learning analysis' for descriptor identification is too generic to tag as a distinct model type. The domain is alloy/materials discovery, best captured by Chemistry with Computational chemistry, with no applicable tier3 term.

The paper trains an SVM classifier on Raman spectra for diagnosis/therapeutic-response prediction and applies LASSO, Random Forest and XGBoost for convergent proteomic feature selection, all supervised learning. The subject is spectrometric/proteomic integration for breast cancer biomarker and drug-mechanism discovery, so Omics with Proteomics and Oncology fits best.

The paper applies a pre-existing multilingual machine learning model to score goal orientations in political text, with no training, fine-tuning, or algorithm named, so model_type/model_family stay empty. The subject (climate policy framing and voter support) is outside the biomedical domain vocabulary, though the text-rating step involves natural language processing.

The paper trains a Random Forest classifier for land-cover mapping and XGBoost regression for spatial LST variance explanation, both supervised learning on the study's own remote-sensing data. SHAP is an explainability method and is excluded, and the domain is environmental/remote-sensing informatics rather than biomedical science.

The paper trains genomic, phenomic, and multiomics prediction models for wheat grain yield, a supervised prediction task, but the abstract names only 'parametric and non-parametric models' without specifying any algorithm or architecture, so model_type and model_family are left empty per the evidence rules.

The paper applies a discovery pipeline combining sequence motif pattern matching with pretrained prediction tools (IUPred3 for disorder, AlphaFold3 for structure) without training any model. Domain is virology/infectious disease, focused on host-viral protein interactions via LC3-interacting region motifs.

The paper's computational content consists of bioinformatics pipelines and network analyses (single-cell transcriptomics, pseudotime, SCENIC, CellChat, NicheNet) plus differential/bulk RNA-seq validation, which are excluded from model_type tagging; no named ML model is trained, fine-tuned, or prompted. The domain is single-cell transcriptomic immunology of diabetic kidney disease.

This is a prospective multi-centre clinical study in oncology evaluating an AI decision-support system for tumour boards, so Medicine/Oncology/Medical informatics with a clinical-studies tag fit best. The pipeline applies LLMs through prompting to generate guideline-based recommendations, with no training or fine-tuning described, hence only prompted use with no learning paradigm.

The paper is a non-biomedical AIOps/root-cause analysis study on social media platform service workflows, so only computer-science-oriented domain terms apply. It trains a dynamic service-dependency-graph approach to rank causes and predict P95 delay, implying a supervised predictive model, but the abstract names no specific algorithm, model type, or family.

The paper trains logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting classifiers on the Telco churn dataset with a binary supervised target, deploying the best model in a dashboard. The subject matter (telecom customer churn) falls outside all biomedical domain vocabularies, so no domain terms apply.

The paper develops and trains CFRDet, a custom lightweight deep object-detection network (attention modules, inverted residual heads), in a supervised manner on a self-built flat jujube fruit image dataset for agricultural field detection. The domain is computer vision applied to agriculture/imaging, and no other named model types are used beyond baselines.

The paper trains period-specific regression models on field-measured LAI/SPAD with Sentinel-2 features, so model use is trained-in-study with supervised (multi-task) learning. The named winning model is multi-task elastic net (MTE), a classical ML method; MIC is feature selection and the other five regression algorithms are unnamed, and remote-sensing crop trait retrieval maps to Biology/Plant biology/Agricultural science.

Five commercial LLMs (GPT-5.2, Grok, DeepSeek, MedGemma, Claude 4.5 Sonnet) were used via standardized prompts, with no weight updates, to generate Angoff standard-setting estimates compared against faculty judges. No models were trained in the study, so learning_paradigm is empty; generalizability theory and t-tests are statistical analyses, not ML models.

ATR-FTIR spectra from IBD biopsy samples were explored unsupervised with PCA and hierarchical clustering, and supervised PLS-based classifiers were trained with nested cross-validation to assess colorectal cancer risk. No pretrained, prompted, or deep models are named, so the families are classical machine learning and dimensionality reduction.

The paper trains neural network regression models on experimental thermal-inactivation data (temperature/time vs. Salmonella log reduction), a supervised prediction task; the abstract gives no indication of a deep architecture, so the plain 'neural network' maps to classic neural network. The domain is food microbiology (Salmonella thermal inactivation in a therapeutic food product), and the 'conventional models' are kinetic/statistical fits rather than named ML models.

The study fine-tunes Esri's pretrained deep learning Solar Panel Detection model on local Brisbane imagery via transfer learning (supervised) for rooftop solar PV mapping, evaluated for trustworthiness under geographic domain shift. No specific architecture is named, so the model is tagged verbatim and no domain_tier3 term applies beyond generic imaging/ML.

The paper trains a domain-adaptive open-vocabulary detection framework built on a dynamic prompt distribution network (a deep neural component) and a density-aware multiple instance learning strategy that exploits weakly supervised image-level tags, so supervised and semi-supervised learning both apply, with adaptation of pretrained open-vocabulary representations. The subject is a computer-vision machine-learning method for food inspection and dietary monitoring, best placed under Computer science / Machine learning with Agricultural science for the food-science application; no tier-3 vocabulary term fits.

The paper trains a Gaussian process (Bayesian) classification model on literature-derived alloy composition descriptors to predict glass-forming ability, a supervised task, and verifies predictions experimentally; the subject is materials/alloy chemistry with a machine-learning methodology focus.

This is a computational phylogenetics software paper (RAxML-NG 2.0) introducing model selection, tree-search heuristics, and branch support metrics. The abstract mentions a machine learning-based branch support prediction model trained by the authors but names no specific algorithm, so model_type and model_family remain empty.

The paper develops a MXene/PDMS piezoresistive sensor (materials/bioengineering domain) and uses a one-dimensional CNN trained on acoustic-vibration signals to achieve 97.5% pitch recognition, i.e. a supervised deep learning model trained in this study.

The paper develops ProteinTalks, pretrained on temporal perturbation proteomics trajectories to learn transferable dynamical latent representations (self-supervised) and adapted for supervised downstream drug-discovery tasks on organoids and biopsies. Domains centre on proteomics-driven in silico drug discovery; no concrete architecture (e.g. transformer) is named in the abstract, so the model is tagged verbatim.

The paper trains XGBoost models on retrospective patient data to predict bacterial infection foci (supervised classification), with Venn-ABERS and conformal prediction serving as calibration/uncertainty-quantification techniques rather than distinct model types. The clinical domain is medicine applied to infectious-disease diagnostics using ML, hence the medical informatics and infectious disease tags.

The study trains machine learning algorithms on baseline steroid and B-cell measurements to predict seroconversion (supervised), but the abstract names no specific algorithm or model family, so model_type/model_family stay empty. Domains center on immunology of influenza vaccination, with single-cell RNA-seq supporting transcriptomic and gene-expression tagging.

The paper applies a prompted LLM within a multiagent orchestration framework to integrate existing metabolite annotation tools (SIRIUS, FLARE, JESTR, DiffMS) with no model training. Domain is metabolomics/analytical chemistry, focused on small-molecule MS/MS annotation and workflow integration.

The paper trains MaxEnt species distribution models on occurrence and climate data (CMIP6) for 13 wild Hordeum species, a supervised non-neural statistical learning method. The subject is ecological niche modeling of plant crop wild relatives, so the domain terms reflect ecology and plant biology with a biodiversity focus.

A microbiome study of rectal cancer patients using shotgun metagenomic sequencing to link oral/gut microbial profiles with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy response. The AI-based prediction model is trained in this study on microbiome plus clinical features, but the abstract names no specific algorithm or architecture, so model_type and model_family remain empty.

The paper trains a semi-supervised cross-lingual ontology induction and NER framework on partially labeled multilingual financial corpora, using confidence-based filtering, multi-view distillation, and an uncertainty-aware contrastive objective, but names no specific model architecture, so model_type is empty. Domain-wise it is an NLP/ontology paper outside the biomedical sphere, best captured by Computer science with NLP and Ontology and terminology at tier 2.

ProRB is a new sequence-based model trained to jointly predict protein-RNA binding affinity, interface contacts and generate RNA sequences, while consuming frozen embeddings from pretrained protein and RNA language models via cross-modal attention (a transformer component). Supervised training is used for the prediction tasks, with deep learning, representation learning (language-model embeddings), and a generative design component as the model families.

The paper fits machine-learning-based feature selection algorithms on transcriptomic data to rank hub genes, but names no specific algorithm or architecture, so model_type and model_family remain empty per the evidence rules. Domains reflect the gene-expression/bioinformatic analysis of ferroptosis-related genes across IBD and periodontitis, with in silico compound screening supporting drug development.

The paper trains an XGBoost model on its own urban PM2.5 and grey-green spatial data, a supervised gradient-boosted tree approach (SHAP is explainability analysis and LISA a spatial statistic, so neither is a model type). The subject is environmental science with a machine-learning methodology; no EDAM tier1 or tier3 term fits this air-quality/urban-planning topic.

The paper's core contribution is materials chemistry (PVDF-based piezoelectric composite fabrication) applied to human physiological monitoring, with no specific algorithm named; the machine learning is used for supervised classification of motion signals, so no model types or families can be tagged from the abstract alone.

The paper trains a hybrid evolutionary-strategy / soft actor-critic controller guided by online simulator feedback (reinforcement learning) and recycles accepted conformations as confidence-weighted pseudo-labels (semi-supervised); the simulator (all-atom molecular dynamics) is an evaluation environment, not a tagged model. Domain terms reflect the protein sequence-structure setting with contact prediction on CASP14 targets.

The paper trains machine-learning interatomic potentials on r2SCAN-level DFT reference data to run molecular dynamics simulations of aluminosilicate glasses, a supervised learning task in computational chemistry; the MLIP type has no assigned family in the canonical list, so model_family is empty.

The study builds gene co-expression modules from peripheral blood transcriptomics and couples them with fALFF imaging features to train a diagnostic classifier for schizophrenia, which is supervised learning on the paper's own data. No specific ML algorithm or model family is named in the abstract (module detection and mediation analyses are pipelines/statistics, not model types), so model_type and model_family are empty.

The paper trains LAANet, a deep network combining a Mamba-style state space model (CMFM) for multimodal fusion with attention modules and a dilated-convolution decoder, on labelled V-D-T salient object detection data (supervised). The subject is a computer-vision machine learning method for imaging, with no biomedical domain terms applicable.

A supervised clinical risk prediction model for MDR infection was trained on MIMIC-IV and external data, with KNN selected as the best of seven algorithms; LASSO was used for feature selection. No pretrained or prompted model is involved, and the only named algorithm besides LASSO is KNN.

A multiple-kernel ridge regression model is trained on GFN1-xTB-computed band gaps of theoretical COFs to learn structure-property relationships, a supervised task in computational/materials chemistry; SOAP descriptors and GFN1-xTB are representation/simulation methods, not learned models.

The study trains four supervised regression models (XGBoost, random forest, SVM, linear regression) on 927 compiled biochar adsorption records to predict heavy-metal uptake capacity, with SHAP and PDP used only for interpretation (excluded as model types). The subject is adsorption/environmental chemistry, so Chemistry at tier 1 and Environmental science at tier 2 fit best.

The paper trains its own deep learning model (Vib2Conf) on labelled spectrum-conformation pairs (QM9S, VB-Mols, QMe14S benchmarks), so the learning is supervised. The abstract names an attentional resampler and Mixture-of-Experts as components/architecture; MoE is tagged as the model type while attention is only a component, and no further algorithm names appear.

A clinical pharmacovigilance-oriented cohort study that trains supervised ML models (best: random forest) to predict rivaroxaban-associated bleeding, with LASSO for feature selection and XGBoost among the evaluated models. SMOTEENN is a resampling technique and SHAP an explainability method, so neither is tagged as a model type.

The paper applies an existing CNN-based visual saliency/attention model as-is, decomposing its convolutional filters into regressors for fMRI GLM analysis, with no model training or fine-tuning reported; the filter grouping into three clusters does not name a specific clustering algorithm, so no additional model type is tagged.

The paper trains fairness-constrained credit scoring models on the Home Credit Default Risk dataset, using AIF360's Reweighing preprocessing and Fairlearn's ExponentiatedGradient (Demographic Parity) and ThresholdOptimizer (Equalized Odds) strategies, all applied within a supervised learning setting. The work is a computer-science/machine-learning study of algorithmic fairness rather than a biomedical one, so no biomedical domain terms apply.

The paper trains random forest and XGBoost models on genetic data (simulations and UK Biobank) to predict disease risk, comparing them against standard additive polygenic risk scores. Both models are gradient/tree ensembles, giving classical machine learning plus ensemble learning families under supervised learning.

The paper trains regularized XGBoost regressors and classifiers on RDKit physicochemical descriptors to predict small-molecule partitioning into biomolecular condensates, a supervised cheminformatics task; SHAP is explainability and RDKit is a descriptor toolkit, so neither is a model type.

DeepSMCA is trained on 914 curated compounds: an unsupervised VGAE learns PPI network embeddings that feed a supervised ResNetDNN synergy classifier, both deep architectures. The Bliss independence model is a statistical drug-interaction reference, not an ML model, so it is excluded.

The paper trains a supervised burned/unburned classifier on Landsat spectral change metrics (ΔNBR, ΔMIRBI, ΔBAI), with a calibrated radial-basis support vector machine as the best-performing model among five evaluated classifiers. The subject is environmental/forest fire monitoring using machine learning, with no other named model types, deep learning, or biomedical domain content.

The paper trains scaffold-aware ML models on its own compound datasets (supervised) and applies pretrained toxicity-endpoint prediction tools as-is, with PCA used to analyse the multidimensional docking profile. Molecular docking is a physics/chemistry method and no specific learning algorithm for the toxicity predictions is named, so model_type is limited to PCA; the domain focus is cheminformatics/toxicology of small-molecule natural products.

The study trained four ML algorithms on plasma proteomics data to select and validate a severity biomarker panel, implying supervised classification. Since the abstract does not name the four algorithms, model_type and model_family are left empty per the evidence rules (Limma is a statistical test, not a model).

The paper fits causal forest algorithms on NHANES-style cross-sectional data to estimate heterogeneous individual-level associations with sarcopenia risk, so the model is trained in-study under a supervised paradigm (causal forest = classical ML + ensemble learning). The clinical focus on diabetes and sarcopenia in adults points to endocrinology/metabolism and geriatric medicine under Medicine.

The paper develops and trains a MAP-EM Gaussian mixture clustering framework (with NIW priors, graph regularization, noise component, and split-merge adaptation) on text corpora, which is unsupervised classical ML. The variational Bayesian GMM is only a comparator, so it is not tagged.

The paper trains/adapts pretrained visual (ViT) and textual (ClinicalBERT) encoders with a supervised multi-label classification head on MIMIC-CXR, fusing both modalities via an adapted Gated Multimodal Unit. Domain is medical imaging AI for thoracic pathology detection combining radiographs and clinical text.

The paper trains supervised regression models on small experimental datasets using physics-derived 3D solvation descriptors to predict battery Coulombic efficiency, but names no specific algorithm, so model_type is left empty. The physics-guided descriptor design places it in physics-informed machine learning within a computational chemistry/electrolyte discovery context.

Four ML algorithms (XGBoost, Random Forest, LASSO, SVM-RFE) were trained on NSCLC transcriptomic data in a supervised manner to identify key genes, while WGCNA provides an unsupervised co-expression step and the pretrained CIBERSORTx tool was applied as-is for immune deconvolution. Molecular docking, MR, and enrichment analyses are excluded as non-ML or statistical methods.

The paper describes an expert system that parses natural-language requirements and generates code, but the abstract names no specific ML model, architecture, or tool, and reports no training, fine-tuning, or prompting of a pretrained model; the NLP algorithms are left unnamed, so model_type and learning_paradigm are empty and only the NLP family is tagged.

The paper develops a fluorescent nanosensor for stress biomarkers and applies PLS-DA (partial least squares discriminant analysis) for multivariate discrimination of dopamine, noradrenaline, and cortisol, which is a supervised classical ML model trained on the paper's own titration data. The domain is analytical/fluorescence chemistry targeting small-molecule biomarkers; no other ML models are named.

A retrospective MIMIC-IV cohort study of myocardial infarction mortality prediction integrating stress hyperglycemia and glycemic variability, with machine learning models (best: Random Forest) trained for supervised risk prediction across glycemic phenotypes. Only Random Forest is named among the five ML algorithms, so it is the sole tagged model type; the other four are unnamed and cannot be tagged.

The paper develops a logistic prediction model based on tumor size and biochemical markers to predict metastasis in insulinoma patients, trained on retrospective cohort data (supervised classification). The subject is endocrine oncology of a rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.

The paper applies AlphaFold2 as a pretrained tool to predict the PimA structure, with no training or fine-tuning of models; molecular docking and mutagenesis are experimental/physics methods, not ML model types. The subject is mycobacterial enzymology and anti-tubercular drug target development.

The paper trains neural-network friction models (predicting friction coefficient, friction factor, or shear stress) on data from sliding compression tests and FE simulations, a supervised regression task in tribology/mechanics, best captured by Physics and Machine learning. The abstract names only 'neural-network-based formulations' without indicating a deep architecture, so 'neural network' with the classic neural network family is used.

A materials-chemistry study (high-nickel cathode degradation) that integrates DFT with machine-learning interatomic potentials trained in-house on DFT data, plus unsupervised clustering to rank electrolyte additives. The MLIP and clustering are the only named model types; DFT itself is not a model type.

The paper trains machine learning-based classification models and QSAR models on compound data for virtual screening of TRPV1 antagonists (supervised learning), with no specific algorithm named beyond the classification/QSAR framing. Molecular dynamics simulations and shape similarity screening are physics/chemistry methods, not ML model types, and the domain centres on computational medicinal chemistry and drug discovery.

The paper trains forecasting models for daily stock log returns, a supervised prediction task, but names no specific algorithm -- only 'deep learning models' versus unspecified 'traditional models' -- so only the deep learning family is taggable and no concrete model type can be listed. The hybrid filter/wrapper feature selection is a preprocessing step, not a model, and the financial domain matches none of the biomedical vocabulary terms.

The paper trains a sample-efficient ML model on engineered Wavelet-transform image features to predict eggshell colour traits in livestock, contrasting this with deep learning that needs large labelled datasets. The abstract names no specific ML algorithm (only 'machine learning'), so only the named Wavelet transform method is tagged, with the learned prediction implying supervised training on their own data.

The study applies Cell Painting high-content imaging with sparse PLS-DA, a supervised multivariate classifier trained on the paper's own morphology features, so partial least squares (classical machine learning, supervised, trained in this study) is the only named model. Domain terms reflect the endothelial cell-biology/toxicology subject; no tier3 term fits the controlled list.

The subject is a computational method for transcriptomics data in pan-cancer/tumor-microenvironment analysis.

The paper integrates multi-omics, PPI networks, single-cell transcriptomics and SHAP-based explanation of an unnamed predictive model linking microbial metabolites to endometriosis risk, so the underlying ML model is trained on the study's own data in a supervised manner but no algorithm is named, leaving model_type/model_family empty (SHAP itself is an explainability method, not a model). Molecular simulations/docking are excluded per model-type rules.

A pharmacovigilance study applying the Bayesian confidence propagation neural network for FAERS disproportionality analysis and LASSO regression for feature refinement, plus an unnamed machine-learning gene-prioritization step (not taggable without a named algorithm). Domains centre on pharmacology/pharmacovigilance with transcriptomic integration.

A surface-science/chemistry study of hydrogen tunneling characterized by STM, with the computational component being deep-learning-assisted path-integral Monte Carlo simulations that identify the tunneling pathway. The deep-learning component is trained on the paper's data (likely a learned potential for the PIMC), but no specific architecture or algorithm is named, so model_type stays empty and only the deep learning family is tagged; the Monte Carlo simulation itself is excluded per the model-type rules.

A cognitive neuroscience fMRI study of trait impression updating, fitting the Biology/Neurobiology domain with functional (MRI-based) neuroimaging as the primary technique. The work is an expert-independent text-mining/NLP framework, best tagged Informatics with NLP and Data mining.

The paper trains a hybrid ML forecasting model for crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks, an ecology/population-dynamics application; the abstract names no specific ML algorithm or architecture, so model_type and model_family are left empty, with supervised learning implied by fitting a forecast model to observational data.

The paper trains an XGBoost model on an ASEAN country-year panel to project NCD burden, alongside PLS structural equation modeling and fixed-effects regression for inferential association testing (fixed-effects regression excluded as association testing only). Domain is population-level non-communicable disease epidemiology with heavy statistical methodology.

The study applies health-risk assessment frameworks (RAGS, KRAG) to fluoride multimedia exposure, an environmental-health/public-health topic, and mentions 'explainable machine learning' without naming any algorithm, so model_type and model_family remain empty. The ML analysis is applied to simulated exposure scenarios (implying a supervised fit within the study), but no architecture or learning detail is given beyond that.

The paper applies single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq to primate testes, fitting clustering (an unsupervised method) on its own integrated datasets, so the model is trained in-study under an unsupervised paradigm. Pseudotime trajectory and differential expression/enrichment analyses are pipeline analyses, not ML model types; no named algorithms beyond clustering appear in the abstract.

REAP trains RankReg, a ranking-regression model with a hybrid ranking/quantitative loss, in a closed loop directly from robotic experimental feedback, which is supervised learning plus active (query-driven, closed-loop) experimentation. The abstract names no concrete underlying architecture, so only the named RankReg framework is tagged as a model type.

The study integrates TCGA transcriptomics with GDSC2 drug sensitivity data, applying the oncoPredict algorithm (a regression-based pharmacogenomic tool) as-is to predict CDK4/6 inhibitor sensitivity, and trains its own machine-learning feature selection on the cohort (paradigm supervised), though no specific algorithm is named so only oncoPredict is listed verbatim. Domain terms reflect the lncRNA/transcriptomic biomarker-discovery focus in breast cancer pharmacogenomics.

The paper trains an MLP on ROSMAP scRNA-seq data to classify AD vs control nuclei and uses its embeddings for disease trajectory inference, so the model is trained in a supervised setting. SHAP, gene regulatory network construction, and trajectory analysis are interpretability/pipeline steps, not model types.
